blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Node classification in heterophilic graphs remains an open problem: aggregating over neighbourhoods can damp precisely the part of the signal that carries the labels. The field has answered with ever more expressive propagation operators, leaving the aggregation step that precedes them fixed by degree normalisation. However, degree normalisation acts as a spectral valley in its own right, attenuating a fixed middle band whose position at lambda equal 1 is set by the normalisation rather than by the data, exactly where the eigenvalues of dense graphs accumulate. We therefore begin with the representations rather than the propagation, in two stages: a learnable aggregation followed by an ordinary spectral filter. The first, SpecValley learns the position, sharpness and flank gains of the valley for every graph. We show formally how the aggregation operator and downstream filter interact. We establish that the response 1 minus lambda of degree normalisation vanishes exactly at that accumulation point. A spectral energy budget shows that what aggregation removes from a band, no linear spectral filter can recover. Crowding alone says nothing about the benefit. That is decided by how much label energy the valley removes, which we measure for every graph. SpecValley achieves strong results across heterophilic benchmarks, and a controlled ablation over aggregation operators and downstream filters attributes the gain to aggregation rather than the filter.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Graphs are a fundamental data structure for relational information: nodes stand
for entities, edges for the relations between them. Node classification is a
central task, with applications in social networks, biological systems and
recommendation settings ( Kipf and Welling, 2017 , Veličković et al., 2018 ) . Graph neural
networks (GNNs) shape this field by propagating and aggregating information
across local neighbourhoods.

blocks.en:
Most GNNs assume homophily, that is, that neighbouring nodes share similar
features or classes ( Zhu et al., 2020 , Pei et al., 2020 ) . In heterophilic
graphs this does not hold ( Yan et al., 2022 ) : repeated aggregation amplifies
mismatched signals and reduces class separability, particularly in dense
graphs ( Oono and Suzuki, 2020 ) . The field has answered with feature-driven
models ( Abu-El-Haija et al., 2019 , Lim et al., 2021 ) , contrastive
learning ( Veličković et al., 2019 , Hassani and Khasahmadi, 2020 , Qiu et al., 2020 ) ,
structure learning ( Franceschi et al., 2019 , Wu et al., 2022 ) and increasingly
elaborate spectral and transformer architectures ( Chien et al., 2021 , Lin et al., 2024 , Koke and Cremers, 2024 , Deng et al., 2024 ) , each tied to a regime:
transformers require large datasets, spectral models excel on small or dense
heterophilic graphs. All of them design the convolution operator or the
structure of the graph and leave the step before it untouched: the filter is
learned, the material it operates on is not.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Standard neighbourhood aggregation amplifies mismatched signals in heterophilic
graphs, causing oversmoothing and reduced class
separability ( Li et al., 2018 , Yan et al., 2022 , Oono and Suzuki, 2020 ) .
Feature-driven methods emphasise multi-hop interactions or decouple features
from topology ( Abu-El-Haija et al., 2019 , Lim et al., 2021 ) ,
structure-oriented methods reweight or denoise edges ( Franceschi et al., 2019 , Wu et al., 2022 ) . Both operate on fixed representations.
Spectral methods such as GPR-GNN ( Chien et al., 2021 ) and
FAGCN ( Bo et al., 2021 ) learn adaptive frequency weights,
BernNet ( He et al., 2021 ) approximates arbitrary filters,
Specformer ( Bo et al., 2023 ) learns the filter with a transformer over
the eigenvalues, JacobiConv ( Wang and Zhang, 2022 ) uses Jacobi polynomial
bases, NLSF ( Lin et al., 2024 ) introduces equivariant nonlinear
filtering. These design expressive operators but apply them to a frequency
profile that the preceding aggregation has already fixed.
Few works address that step itself, and they do so spatially: separating ego
from neighbourhood information ( Zhu et al., 2020 , Platonov et al., 2023 ) ,
projecting along and against the edge direction ( Rossi et al., 2023 ) or
learning edge weights by attention ( Veličković et al., 2018 ) . Read spectrally,
ego-neighbour separation yields the affine family a + b ⁡ ( 1 − λ ) a+b\,(1-\lambda) , so the
position of the response is learnable but its shape is not: sharpness and
asymmetry remain those of degree normalisation. Attention weights are not a function of L L , and our ablation measures how they compare with degree normalisation (Section 5.2 ).
Graph transformers inject global structure at the feature level via Laplacian or
random-walk encodings ( Dwivedi et al., 2022 , Rampášek et al., 2022 , Kreuzer et al., 2021 ) and Polynormer ( Deng et al., 2024 ) combines polynomial expressivity with local and global attention.

blocks.en:
We evaluate our method on node classification in dense relational
graphs, using six heterophilic benchmarks: Squirrel-f, Chameleon-f,
Actor, Crocodile ( Rozemberczki et al., 2021 ) , Tolokers ( Platonov et al., 2023 ) and HM-categories ( Bazhenov et al., 2025 ) (Table 2 ). Squirrel-f and Chameleon-f are the
node-deduplicated variants of Platonov et al. (2023) , which remove the
train–test leakage caused by duplicated pages, and are used in place of the
originals for comparison with prior work ( Lin et al., 2024 ) . Crocodile is a
denser Wikipedia network from the same source, whose published target is
continuous and which we discretise into five equally sized classes, as done for
Chameleon and Squirrel by Pei et al. (2020) and on this graph
by Xiao et al. (2023) .
The selection spans more than an order of magnitude in size and degree and
deliberately covers two spectral regimes. On Squirrel-f, Chameleon-f, Crocodile
and HM-categories, neighbourhood aggregation clearly improves over the
feature-only baseline (Table 3 ), so label information is
recoverable by spectral denoising. On Actor and Tolokers it is not: Actor is
sparse with a label spectrum close to that of noise
(Section 4.3 ), while Tolokers, and in part
HM-categories, carry label information at the level of individual nodes, where
models that separate ego from neighbour information and attention-based
architectures perform best ( Platonov et al., 2023 , Bazhenov et al., 2025 ) .
Covering both regimes lets us attribute gains and failures to the spectral
structure of a graph rather than to the choice of benchmarks.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
The aggregation step that precedes every graph filter is a spectral operator
in its own right, and on dense graphs its fixed zero falls exactly where the
eigenvalues accumulate. Making this step learnable is enough to change the
outcome: SpecValley, a learned valley in front of an unchanged ChebNet,
is the best
on four of six heterophilic benchmarks and within the confidence interval of the best on a fifth,
and the ablation over aggregators and filters
shows that no downstream filter closes the gap on its own. The label-energy
spectrum explains where the valley helps and where, as on Actor, no spectral
aggregator can.

blocks.en:
Limitations and Future Work. Our analysis is confined to dense heterophilic graphs with informative
spectral structure and to the linear part of the pipeline; ReLU and layer
normalisation can move energy between modes, and the operator parameters are
fitted on half of the validation set. Two questions remain open: when
attention before propagation aligns with the spectrum and when it learns
node-specific weights, and why a Chebyshev filter does not reproduce the gain
of the valley by itself, although the composition of valley and filter is a
polynomial of only one order higher.

All models are trained from scratch on each split, with hidden dimension 64 64 ,
input dimension equal to the number of node features and output dimension equal

decay 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} ) on the cross-entropy loss, with dropout 0.5 0.5 in the
aggregation stage and in every downstream layer; on Tolokers, the only binary
task, the loss is class-weighted by the inverse class ratio. Nodes without a
label are excluded from all masks. All six graphs are treated as undirected;
where the source provides directed edges, we symmetrise them before computing L L , so that S = S ⊤ = P sym S=S^{\top}=P_{\mathrm{sym}} in Eq. ( 3 ).
We evaluate after every epoch and report the test score of the epoch with the best validation score; the test labels enter no
selection at any point. Table 5 summarises the protocol of the
three measurements.
